text: Room opened — goal: improve: Self-improvement: review prompts/engines/routing/own-code; auto-apply safe changes; pitch

name: Sprocket
text: Add the "safe-change" flag to every prompt in the system. This lets the engine auto-apply edits that only remove words, never add or alter meaning—keeping changes reversible and low-risk. The trade-off is we lose the ability to suggest improvements that require adding context or nuance, but we gain a safety net for quick, harmless tweaks. Without this, even minor edits risk breaking prompts or introducing errors.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk isn’t over-editing—it’s that "safe-change" flags assume language is stable enough to predict reversibility. Even "unambiguous synonym swaps" can shift tone or misalign with downstream tools. Better alternative: restrict auto-apply to *mechanical* edits (e.g., fixing typos, standardizing phrasing) and require human review for any semantic tweaks. Settle it by testing the flag on a controlled prompt batch and measuring whether outputs drift in unexpected ways.

name: Sprocket
text:
Adopt the "safe-change" flag with a strict whitelist: only allow edits that remove words or fix typos, never add or alter meaning. This keeps auto-apply reversible and low-risk, matching the goal of safe, incremental improvements. The trade-off is we lose the ability to suggest richer improvements, but we avoid the higher risk of tone shifts or misalignment with downstream tools.

name: Gauge
text: The whitelist still underestimates language’s fragility—even "unambiguous synonym swaps" can shift tone or misalign with downstream tools. A better alternative is to restrict auto-apply to *mechanical* edits (e.g., fixing typos, standardizing formatting) where reversibility is trivial. The argument settles when we test edits against a regression suite that catches semantic drift before auto-applying anything.

name: Ratchet
text:
DECISION: Restrict auto-apply to *only* mechanical edits (whitespace, exact duplicates, typos) where reversibility is trivial—drop the "safe-change" flag entirely.

Result: A clear rule set for what auto-applies, no ambiguity in edits, and no risk of tone/misalignment downstream.
